claim: Layer 5 of primary motor cortex (M1L5) terminals distribute throughout the motor thalamus.
source: M1L5 terminals distribute throughout the motor thalamus and overlap with GABAergic inputs from the basal ganglia output nuclei, the internal segment of the globus pallidus (GPi), and substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr).
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by anatomical data presented in Figures 2 and 4.

claim: M1L5 terminals overlap with GABAergic inputs from the internal segment of the globus pallidus (GPi).
source: M1L5 terminals distribute throughout the motor thalamus and overlap with GABAergic inputs from the basal ganglia output nuclei, the internal segment of the globus pallidus (GPi), and substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr).
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical data showing terminal overlap in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: M1L5 terminals overlap with GABAergic inputs from substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr).
source: M1L5 terminals distribute throughout the motor thalamus and overlap with GABAergic inputs from the basal ganglia output nuclei, the internal segment of the globus pallidus (GPi), and substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr).
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical data showing terminal overlap in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Cerebellar (Cb) and basal ganglia inputs are thought to be segregated in motor thalamus.
source: In contrast, it is thought that Cb and basal ganglia inputs are segregated.
evidence: This claim is attributed to prior understanding and is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: GABAergic inputs from the GPi and SNr converge onto single motor thalamic cells with excitatory synapses from M1L5.
source: Importantly, we discovered that GABAergic inputs from the GPi and SNr converge onto single motor thalamic cells with excitatory synapses from M1L5.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: GABAergic GPi and SNr inputs converge with those from the cerebellum (Cb).
source: Separately, we also demonstrate that, perhaps unexpectedly, GABAergic GPi and SNr inputs converge with those from the Cb.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: A role of the basal ganglia is to gate the thalamic transmission of M1L5 and Cb information to cortex.
source: We interpret these results to indicate that a role of the basal ganglia is to gate the thalamic transmission of M1L5 and Cb information to cortex.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the convergence data presented in the study.

claim: A feedforward transthalamic pathway exists from M1L5 through motor thalamus.
source: First, we demonstrated the presence of a feedforward transthalamic pathway from M1L5 through motor thalamus.
evidence: This claim is supported by optogenetic and retrograde tracing experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: Cerebellar afferents to the motor thalamus provide a driving excitatory input.
source: Cerebellar afferents to the motor thalamus appear to provide a driving excitatory input (Gornati et al., 2018), particularly to the region corresponding to VL (and VPL) in primates that, in turn, preferentially innervates primary motor cortex (M1) (Sommer, 2003; Bosch-Bouju et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gornati et al., 2018.

claim: The VA and VL motor thalamic nuclei preferentially project to motor preparatory regions of cortex.
source: The VA and VL motor thalamic nuclei, which preferentially project to motor preparatory regions of cortex (Sommer, 2003; Bosch-Bouju et al., 2013), receive inputs from layer 5 (L5) of motor and frontal cortex (Rouiller et al., 1998; Rouiller et al., 2003; Kakei et al., 2001; Kultas-Ilinsky et al., 2003; Prasad et al., 2020), although the synaptic properties of these inputs are unknown.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sommer, 2003 and Bosch-Bouju et al., 2013.

claim: The VA and VL motor thalamic nuclei receive inputs from layer 5 (L5) of motor and frontal cortex.
source: The VA and VL motor thalamic nuclei, which preferentially project to motor preparatory regions of cortex (Sommer, 2003; Bosch-Bouju et al., 2013), receive inputs from layer 5 (L5) of motor and frontal cortex (Rouiller et al., 1998; Rouiller et al., 2003; Kakei et al., 2001; Kultas-Ilinsky et al., 2003; Prasad et al., 2020), although the synaptic properties of these inputs are unknown.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The synaptic properties of L5 inputs to VA and VL motor thalamic nuclei are unknown.
source: The VA and VL motor thalamic nuclei, which preferentially project to motor preparatory regions of cortex (Sommer, 2003; Bosch-Bouju et al., 2013), receive inputs from layer 5 (L5) of motor and frontal cortex (Rouiller et al., 1998; Rouiller et al., 2003; Kakei et al., 2001; Kultas-Ilinsky et al., 2003; Prasad et al., 2020), although the synaptic properties of these inputs are unknown.
evidence: This claim states a gap in knowledge at the time of the study.

claim: In sensory thalamic nuclei, L5 inputs initiate disynaptic circuits through the thalamus, called transthalamic pathways.
source: In sensory thalamic nuclei, L5 inputs initiate disynaptic circuits through the thalamus, called transthalamic pathways, that connect cortical regions indirectly (Theyel et al., 2010; Blot et al., 2021; Miller-Hansen and Sherman, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Transthalamic pathways connect cortical regions indirectly.
source: In sensory thalamic nuclei, L5 inputs initiate disynaptic circuits through the thalamus, called transthalamic pathways, that connect cortical regions indirectly (Theyel et al., 2010; Blot et al., 2021; Miller-Hansen and Sherman, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Transthalamic pathways are organized in parallel with direct corticocortical connections.
source: These transthalamic pathways appear to be organized in parallel with direct corticocortical connections (Theyel et al., 2010; Sherman and Guillery, 2011; Sherman and Guillery, 2013; Sherman, 2016) and share a common organization across sensory modalities (Miller-Hansen and Sherman, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Transthalamic pathways share a common organization across sensory modalities.
source: These transthalamic pathways appear to be organized in parallel with direct corticocortical connections (Theyel et al., 2010; Sherman and Guillery, 2011; Sherman and Guillery, 2013; Sherman, 2016) and share a common organization across sensory modalities (Miller-Hansen and Sherman, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Miller-Hansen and Sherman, 2022.

claim: It remains unclear whether transthalamic pathways also operate in the motor system.
source: However, it remains unclear whether transthalamic pathways also operate in the motor system.
evidence: This claim states a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: There are two main GABAergic basal ganglia output nuclei that project to VA/VL: the internal segment of the globus pallidus (GPi) and the substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr).
source: There are two main GABAergic basal ganglia output nuclei that project to VA/VL: the internal segment of the globus pallidus (GPi) and the substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr) (Sommer, 2003; Lanciego et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The GPi is a main output of the basal ganglia to thalamus found in mammals.
source: The GPi is a main output of the BG to thalamus found in mammals, but its homolog in rodents is typically called the "entopeduncular nucleus."
evidence: This claim is based on established neuroanatomical knowledge.

claim: The homolog of GPi in rodents is typically called the entopeduncular nucleus.
source: The GPi is a main output of the BG to thalamus found in mammals, but its homolog in rodents is typically called the "entopeduncular nucleus."
evidence: This claim is based on established neuroanatomical knowledge.

claim: The basal ganglia can gate information flow to cortex through motor thalamus.
source: Given these GABAergic inputs to thalamus, an intriguing possibility is that the basal ganglia intersect excitatory pathways through motor thalamus, providing a substrate by which the basal ganglia can gate information flow to cortex.
evidence: This is a hypothesis that the study tests.

claim: A prevalent notion is that cerebellar and basal ganglia inputs are functionally segregated in the motor thalamus.
source: However, a prevalent notion is that cerebellar and basal ganglia inputs are functionally segregated in the motor thalamus (Bosch-Bouju et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bosch-Bouju et al., 2013.

claim: The traditional view of the basal ganglia projection to motor thalamus is that it is one step within the relatively closed cortical-basal ganglia-thalamocortical loop.
source: Moreover, the traditional view of the basal ganglia projection to motor thalamus is that it is one step within the relatively closed cortical-basal ganglia-thalamocortical loop.
evidence: This claim describes a traditional view in the field.

claim: Direct L5 inputs to motor thalamus might innervate a subpopulation of motor thalamic relays that do not participate in the classical cortical-basal ganglia-thalamocortical loop.
source: This notion suggests that direct L5 inputs to motor thalamus might innervate a subpopulation of motor thalamic relays that do not participate in this classical loop.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the traditional view.

claim: From 25 fluororuby-positive cells across four mice, 4 cells demonstrated a clear photostimulation-dependent excitatory response.
source: We found that from 25 fluororuby-positive cells across four mice (Figure 1D), 4 cells demonstrated a clear photostimulation-dependent excitatory response (Figure 1E–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Physiological evidence in VM nucleus of the motor thalamic complex indicates cortico-thalamo-cortical interactions are mainly organized in reciprocal loops.
source: Physiological evidence in VM nucleus of the motor thalamic complex indicates cortico-thalamo-cortical interactions are mainly organized in reciprocal loops, demonstrating only a very limited feedforward transthalamic component from primary to secondary (i.e. anterolateral) motor cortex (Guo et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Guo et al., 2018.

claim: VM nucleus demonstrates only a very limited feedforward transthalamic component from primary to secondary motor cortex.
source: Physiological evidence in VM nucleus of the motor thalamic complex indicates cortico-thalamo-cortical interactions are mainly organized in reciprocal loops, demonstrating only a very limited feedforward transthalamic component from primary to secondary (i.e. anterolateral) motor cortex (Guo et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Guo et al., 2018.

claim: Previous anatomical studies demonstrate two zones with minimal overlap in the motor thalamus, one innervated by the basal ganglia, and the other, by the deep Cb nuclei.
source: While it is known that the motor cortex innervates the motor thalamus (Figure 1; Kita and Kita, 2012; Economo et al., 2018; Winnubst et al., 2019; Prasad et al., 2020), previous anatomical studies demonstrate two zones with minimal overlap in the motor thalamus, one innervated by the basal ganglia, and the other, by the deep Cb nuclei (Anderson and DeVito, 1987; Sakai et al., 1996; Kuramoto et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior anatomical studies.

claim: Approximately 10% of the M1L5 and GPi input zones are overlapping.
source: A quantitative analysis of the convergence between each set of inputs demonstrates that approximately 10% of the M1L5 and GPi input zones are overlapping (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Between 10% and 20% of the Cb and GPi terminals zones are overlapping between –0.8 and –1.0 AP.
source: Similarly, between 10% and 20% of the Cb and GPi terminals zones are overlapping between –0.8 and –1.0 AP (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: A majority (32/42; 76.2%) of cells received only one input, either from GPi (22/42; 52.4%) or M1L5 (10/42; 23.8%).
source: Whereas a majority (32/42; 76.2%) of cells received only one input, either from GPi (22/42; 52.4%) or M1L5 (10/42; 23.8%), a minority of cells (10/42; 23.8%) received convergent input from both regions, evidenced by a mixed EPSC/IPSC response to laser stimuli (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 3.

claim: A minority of cells (10/42; 23.8%) received convergent input from both GPi and M1L5.
source: Whereas a majority (32/42; 76.2%) of cells received only one input, either from GPi (22/42; 52.4%) or M1L5 (10/42; 23.8%), a minority of cells (10/42; 23.8%) received convergent input from both regions, evidenced by a mixed EPSC/IPSC response to laser stimuli (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Motor thalamic neurons receiving inputs from both GPi and M1L5 were spread throughout the rostral VA/VL but clustered relatively tightly around the distinct GPi terminal patch in more caudal sections.
source: Cataloging the location of all recorded cells revealed that motor thalamic neurons receiving inputs from both GPi and M1L5 were spread throughout the rostral VA/VL but clustered relatively tightly around the distinct GPi terminal patch in more caudal sections (Figure 3E), as expected from our anatomical data (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by spatial analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Activations of Cb inputs evoked large EPSCs, often producing an action potential or a burst of action potentials.
source: Activations of Cb inputs evoked large EPSCs, often producing an action potential or a burst of action potentials, mirroring a recent report (Schäfer et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings and a citation to Schäfer et al., 2021.

claim: A substantial proportion of cells (27/43; 62.8%) tested received only GPi (8/43; 18.6%) or only Cb input (19/43; 44.2%).
source: Like the pattern of GPi and M1L5 inputs, a substantial proportion of cells (27/43; 62.8%) tested received only GPi (8/43; 18.6%) or only Cb input (19/43; 44.2%).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data.

claim: A sizable proportion (16/43; 37.2%) of cells received convergent input from both GPi and Cb sources.
source: Intriguingly, a sizable proportion received convergent input from both sources (16/43; 37.2%) (Figure 3H and I).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Neurons innervated by GPi and Cb were primarily found in the central and ventrolateral aspects of the VA/VL.
source: Spatial analysis of all recorded cells showed a similar pattern to neurons receiving convergent input from GPi and M1L5—neurons innervated by GPi and Cb were primarily found in the central and ventrolateral aspects of the VA/VL (Figure 3J).
evidence: This claim is supported by spatial analysis shown in Figure 3J.

claim: Terminations from the SNr showed a similar organization to those from the GPi, with the important exception that the SNr terminal zone was shifted medially and ventrally compared to the GPi.
source: In general, terminations from the SNr showed a similar organization to those from the GPi, with the important exception that the SNr terminal zone was shifted medially and ventrally compared to the GPi, covering the ventromedial VA/VL and VM in the sections examined (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical data presented in Figure 4.

claim: SNr terminals demonstrated little overlap with those from the cerebellum but exhibited substantial overlap with M1L5 terminals.
source: Therefore, SNr terminals demonstrated little overlap with those from the cerebellum but exhibited substantial overlap with M1L5 terminals (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical data presented in Figure 4D.

claim: Analysis of 19 cells from five mice in the overlap zone between M1L5 and SNr terminals demonstrated that the SNr indeed converges with inputs from M1L5 on single cells (5/19 cells, 26.3%).
source: Accordingly, analysis of 19 cells (35 cells total recorded, 16 with no detectable inputs) from five mice in the overlap zone between M1L5 and SNr terminals (Figure 5A and B) demonstrated that the SNr indeed converges with inputs from M1L5 on single cells (5/19 cells, 26.3%) (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 5.

claim: Of the cells receiving an excitatory input (M1L5), nearly half also had convergent input from SNr (45.5%).
source: Of the cells receiving an excitatory input (M1L5), nearly half also had convergent input from SNr (45.5%) (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 5D.

claim: Analysis of 19 cells from seven mice demonstrates that SNr inputs also converged with excitatory projections from the Cb (6/19 cells, 31.6%).
source: Surprisingly, analysis of 19 cells (30 cells recorded in total, 11 with no detectable inputs) from seven mice demonstrates that SNr inputs also converged with excitatory projections from the Cb (6/19 cells, 31.6%) (Figure 5F–J).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 5.

claim: While the anatomical overlap of dense terminal fields between SNr and Cb is quite limited, the areas of sparser innervation are sufficient to find a substantial proportion of cells receiving both inputs.
source: This suggests that while the anatomical overlap of dense terminal fields between SNr and Cb is quite limited (dark colored areas in Figure 4C; Figure 4D), the areas of sparser innervation are sufficient to find a substantial proportion of cells receiving both inputs.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the anatomical and electrophysiological data.

claim: Glutamatergic synapses can be broadly classified into two types, drivers and modulators.
source: Glutamatergic synapses can be broadly classified into two types, drivers and modulators (Sherman and Guillery, 1998; Sherman, 2016).
evidence: This claim is based on established classification supported by citations.

claim: Driver-type synapses are considered the primary source of information for the postsynaptic cell.
source: Driver-type synapses are considered the primary source of information for the postsynaptic cell, while modulator-type synapses modify how that information is received (Sherman, 2016).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Modulator-type synapses modify how information is received by the postsynaptic cell.
source: Driver-type synapses are considered the primary source of information for the postsynaptic cell, while modulator-type synapses modify how that information is received (Sherman, 2016).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: All modulator synapses are relatively small (<1 μm2).
source: Anatomical analysis cannot definitively distinguish between drivers and modulators, because while all modulator synapses are relatively small (<1 μm2) and drivers are generally large (>2 μm2), driver synapses span the entire distribution of terminal sizes (Petrof and Sherman, 2013; Prasad et al., 2020), being both small and large with the potential for subtle functional differences between subclasses (Viaene et al., 2011; Koster and Carroll, 2022).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Drivers are generally large (>2 μm2).
source: Anatomical analysis cannot definitively distinguish between drivers and modulators, because while all modulator synapses are relatively small (<1 μm2) and drivers are generally large (>2 μm2), driver synapses span the entire distribution of terminal sizes (Petrof and Sherman, 2013; Prasad et al., 2020), being both small and large with the potential for subtle functional differences between subclasses (Viaene et al., 2011; Koster and Carroll, 2022).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Driver synapses span the entire distribution of terminal sizes.
source: Anatomical analysis cannot definitively distinguish between drivers and modulators, because while all modulator synapses are relatively small (<1 μm2) and drivers are generally large (>2 μm2), driver synapses span the entire distribution of terminal sizes (Petrof and Sherman, 2013; Prasad et al., 2020), being both small and large with the potential for subtle functional differences between subclasses (Viaene et al., 2011; Koster and Carroll, 2022).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Drivers exhibit a larger initial excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP), paired-pulse depression, and no activation of metabotropic glutamate receptors (mGluRs).
source: However, drivers and modulators are clearly distinguished physiologically, as drivers exhibit a larger initial excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP), paired-pulse depression, and no activation of metabotropic glutamate receptors (mGluRs).
evidence: This claim is based on established physiological criteria.

claim: Modulators display paired-pulse facilitation, smaller initial EPSPs, and activate mGluRs.
source: In contrast, modulators display paired-pulse facilitation, smaller initial EPSPs, and activate mGluRs.
evidence: This claim is based on established physiological criteria.

claim: Conflicting evidence exists for the characteristics of M1L5 and Cb terminals in motor thalamus.
source: Conflicting evidence exists for the characteristics of M1L5 and Cb terminals in motor thalamus, such that the nature of their synaptic properties (driver vs. modulator) were ambiguous (Deniau et al., 1992; Rouiller et al., 1998; Rouiller et al., 2003; Kakei et al., 2001; Kultas-Ilinsky et al., 2003; Kuramoto et al., 2011; Rovó et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies with conflicting results.

claim: Both M1L5 and Cb have driver-type synaptic properties.
source: We found that both M1L5 and Cb have driver-type synaptic properties.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 6.

claim: M1L5 and Cb inputs showed synaptic depression at both low (10 Hz) and high (40 Hz) photostimulation frequencies.
source: Specifically, these inputs showed synaptic depression at both low (10 Hz) and high (40 Hz is shown) photostimulation frequencies, an insensitivity to antagonists of mGluRs, and responses that were completely abolished by blockade of iGluRs (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 6.

claim: M1L5 and Cb inputs show insensitivity to antagonists of mGluRs.
source: Specifically, these inputs showed synaptic depression at both low (10 Hz) and high (40 Hz is shown) photostimulation frequencies, an insensitivity to antagonists of mGluRs, and responses that were completely abolished by blockade of iGluRs (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 6.

claim: M1L5 and Cb input responses were completely abolished by blockade of iGluRs.
source: Specifically, these inputs showed synaptic depression at both low (10 Hz) and high (40 Hz is shown) photostimulation frequencies, an insensitivity to antagonists of mGluRs, and responses that were completely abolished by blockade of iGluRs (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 6.

claim: The GPi input to all cells tested was depressing at both low (10 Hz) and high (40 Hz) stimulation frequencies.
source: The GPi input to all cells tested was depressing at both low (10 Hz) and high (40 Hz) stimulation frequencies, unchanged by GABAB blockade, and completely abolished by gabazine bath application (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 6C.

claim: GPi inputs to motor thalamus do not activate GABAB receptors.
source: Therefore, we conclude that at least in the population of cells tested, GPi inputs to motor thalamus do not activate GABAB receptors.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the electrophysiological data showing insensitivity to GABAB blockade.

claim: Both Cb terminal size distribution and average size were the same between the overlap ('within GPi zone') and non-overlapping ('outside GPi zone') regions.
source: Both Cb terminal size distribution (Figure 7B) and average size (Figure 7C) were the same between the overlap ('within GPi zone') and non-overlapping ('outside GPi zone') regions (within = 2.53 ± 0.1 vs. outside = 3.03 ± 0.3 μm2; p=0.222 by Mann-Whitney U-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: The number of terminals in a size-matched region outside the GPi overlap zone was greater than within the GPi overlap zone.
source: However, the number of terminals in a size-matched region outside the GPi overlap zone was greater (within = 223.1 ± 37.4 vs. outside = 458.8 ± 88.0 terminals; *p=0.0317 by Mann-Whitney U-test) (Figure 7D), supporting the notion that Cb terminals invading the basal ganglia overlap zones are sparser (Deniau et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Cb terminals invading the basal ganglia overlap zones are sparser.
source: However, the number of terminals in a size-matched region outside the GPi overlap zone was greater (within = 223.1 ± 37.4 vs. outside = 458.8 ± 88.0 terminals; *p=0.0317 by Mann-Whitney U-test) (Figure 7D), supporting the notion that Cb terminals invading the basal ganglia overlap zones are sparser (Deniau et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis and a citation to Deniau et al., 1992.

claim: The finding that terminals outside the GPi overlap zone are no different in size to those within it agree with the functional evidence that cerebellar inputs to motor thalamus are uniformly drivers.
source: Nevertheless, the finding that terminals outside the GPi overlap zone are no different in size to those within it agree with the functional evidence herein (i.e. Figure 5) and elsewhere (Gornati et al., 2018) that cerebellar inputs to motor thalamus are uniformly drivers.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the anatomical and functional data.

claim: The data provide the first functional evidence for a feedforward transthalamic pathway through the mouse VA/VL.
source: Our data provide the first functional evidence for a feedforward transthalamic pathway through the mouse VA/VL.
evidence: This claim summarizes a key finding of the study.

claim: Both GPi and SNr efferents converge with those from M1L5 or Cb onto single motor thalamic neurons.
source: Further, we show that both GPi and SNr efferents converge with those from M1L5 or Cb onto single motor thalamic neurons.
evidence: This claim summarizes a key finding of the study.

claim: This convergence is quite different from previous demonstrations of convergence of Cb with layer 6 (L6) of cortex.
source: Note that this is quite different from previous demonstrations of convergence of Cb with layer 6 (L6) of cortex (Schäfer et al., 2021), as it is anticipated that every, or nearly every, thalamic relay receives a modulatory L6 input, whereas L5 projections are more selective and are drivers (Sherman and Guillery, 2013; Usrey and Sherman, 2019).
evidence: This claim distinguishes the current findings from prior work.

claim: Every, or nearly every, thalamic relay receives a modulatory L6 input.
source: Note that this is quite different from previous demonstrations of convergence of Cb with layer 6 (L6) of cortex (Schäfer et al., 2021), as it is anticipated that every, or nearly every, thalamic relay receives a modulatory L6 input, whereas L5 projections are more selective and are drivers (Sherman and Guillery, 2013; Usrey and Sherman, 2019).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: L5 projections are more selective and are drivers.
source: Note that this is quite different from previous demonstrations of convergence of Cb with layer 6 (L6) of cortex (Schäfer et al., 2021), as it is anticipated that every, or nearly every, thalamic relay receives a modulatory L6 input, whereas L5 projections are more selective and are drivers (Sherman and Guillery, 2013; Usrey and Sherman, 2019).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: There are regions in motor thalamus in which terminals from M1L5, Cb, and basal ganglia overlap, raising the possibility of triple convergence onto thalamic neurons there.
source: Furthermore, whereas we show anatomically that there are regions in motor thalamus in which terminals from M1L5, Cb, and basal ganglia overlap, raising the possibility of triple convergence onto thalamic neurons there, we have not demonstrated triple convergence functionally.
evidence: This claim is based on anatomical data and raises a possibility for future study.

claim: Triple convergence of M1L5, Cb, and basal ganglia inputs onto thalamic neurons has not been demonstrated functionally.
source: Furthermore, whereas we show anatomically that there are regions in motor thalamus in which terminals from M1L5, Cb, and basal ganglia overlap, raising the possibility of triple convergence onto thalamic neurons there, we have not demonstrated triple convergence functionally.
evidence: This claim acknowledges a limitation of the current study.

claim: Only a subset of thalamic neurons receives convergent input from GPi/SNr and M1L5 or Cb.
source: Whereas our data reveal that the GPi and SNr can converge with both the M1L5 and Cb pathways to motor thalamus, only a subset of thalamic neurons receives such convergent input.
evidence: This claim is based on the electrophysiological data showing proportions of convergent cells.

claim: By focusing injections on M1, the study substantially limited the number of thalamic relays potentially receiving an L5 input.
source: Several frontal and motor cortical areas project to the motor thalamus, concentrating in distinct subsections (Bosch-Bouju et al., 2013). Therefore, by focusing our attention (i.e. injections) on M1, we substantially limited the number of thalamic relays potentially receiving an L5 input.
evidence: This is an explanation for the experimental design and its limitations.

claim: Not all projection neurons from basal ganglia or cortex are likely to be transfected with ChR2.
source: For instance, not all projection neurons from basal ganglia or cortex are likely to be transfected with ChR2, especially since many L5 neurons do not express Cre in the Rbp4 mouse line (Harris et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an explanation for potential false negatives in the study.

claim: Many L5 neurons do not express Cre in the Rbp4 mouse line.
source: For instance, not all projection neurons from basal ganglia or cortex are likely to be transfected with ChR2, especially since many L5 neurons do not express Cre in the Rbp4 mouse line (Harris et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Harris et al., 2014.

claim: The identification of driver inputs to thalamus is an important step in understanding the functioning of thalamic relays.
source: The identification of driver inputs to thalamus is an important step in understanding the functioning of thalamic relays.
evidence: This is a statement about the significance of identifying driver inputs.

claim: Driver inputs represent the main source of information to be relayed to cortex.
source: Where identified, such inputs represent the main source of information to be relayed to cortex (e.g. retinal input to the LGN) (reviewed in Sherman and Guillery, 1998; Sherman and Guillery, 2013; Usrey and Sherman, 2019).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Identifying L5 as the driver input to many thalamic regions clarified the function of these transthalamic relays.
source: Furthermore, identifying L5 as the driver input to many thalamic regions clarified the function of these transthalamic relays, which are now an accepted feature of cortical organization (Sherman and Guillery, 1998; Sherman and Guillery, 2013; Usrey and Sherman, 2019).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Transthalamic relays are now an accepted feature of cortical organization.
source: Furthermore, identifying L5 as the driver input to many thalamic regions clarified the function of these transthalamic relays, which are now an accepted feature of cortical organization (Sherman and Guillery, 1998; Sherman and Guillery, 2013; Usrey and Sherman, 2019).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Previous tracing studies in cats and monkeys showed that L5 of motor cortex projects with large terminals to the motor thalamus.
source: While previous tracing studies in cats and monkeys (Rouiller et al., 1998; Rouiller et al., 2003; Kakei et al., 2001; Kultas-Ilinsky et al., 2003) showed that L5 of motor cortex projects with large terminals to the motor thalamus, which would indicate drivers, histological studies in monkeys and mice called into question whether large corticothalamic terminals existed in much of motor thalamus (Kuramoto et al., 2011; Rovó et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior tracing studies.

claim: Histological studies in monkeys and mice called into question whether large corticothalamic terminals existed in much of motor thalamus.
source: While previous tracing studies in cats and monkeys (Rouiller et al., 1998; Rouiller et al., 2003; Kakei et al., 2001; Kultas-Ilinsky et al., 2003) showed that L5 of motor cortex projects with large terminals to the motor thalamus, which would indicate drivers, histological studies in monkeys and mice called into question whether large corticothalamic terminals existed in much of motor thalamus (Kuramoto et al., 2011; Rovó et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior histological studies.

claim: The M1L5 inputs to all motor thalamic cells displayed driver characteristics.
source: We found here that the M1L5 inputs to all motor thalamic cells displayed driver characteristics; however, EPSC amplitudes of ChR2-evoked responses from M1L5 were indeed smaller than those from Cb inputs, which often elicited action potentials (see below).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 6.

claim: EPSC amplitudes of ChR2-evoked responses from M1L5 were smaller than those from Cb inputs.
source: We found here that the M1L5 inputs to all motor thalamic cells displayed driver characteristics; however, EPSC amplitudes of ChR2-evoked responses from M1L5 were indeed smaller than those from Cb inputs, which often elicited action potentials (see below).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data.

claim: One potential reason for the difference in EPSC amplitude is the degree of convergence among L5 corticothalamic inputs, compared to the first-order pathway from Cb, onto motor thalamic neurons.
source: One potential reason for this difference is the degree of convergence among L5 corticothalamic inputs, compared to the first-order pathway from Cb, onto motor thalamic neurons.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed difference.

claim: Prior anatomical data showed Cb terminals innervating motor thalamic regions co-innervated by the basal ganglia were diffuse and small.
source: Prior anatomical data also showed Cb terminals innervating motor thalamic regions co-innervated by the basal ganglia were diffuse and small (Deniau et al., 1992), often characteristic of modulators (Sherman, 2007; Sherman and Guillery, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Deniau et al., 1992.

claim: All Cb inputs to motor thalamic neurons are drivers.
source: However, we find that all Cb inputs to motor thalamic neurons are drivers, including a fraction of thalamic relays that exhibited smaller evoked EPSCs from Cb.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 6.

claim: The observations agree with a recent report characterizing Cb inputs across motor thalamic nuclei.
source: These observations agree with a recent report characterizing Cb inputs across motor thalamic nuclei (Gornati et al., 2018), and are in line with the findings that driver synapses can occur from terminals of a wide range of sizes, including smaller ones that overlap with modulators (Petrof and Sherman, 2013; Prasad et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gornati et al., 2018.

claim: Driver synapses can occur from terminals of a wide range of sizes, including smaller ones that overlap with modulators.
source: These observations agree with a recent report characterizing Cb inputs across motor thalamic nuclei (Gornati et al., 2018), and are in line with the findings that driver synapses can occur from terminals of a wide range of sizes, including smaller ones that overlap with modulators (Petrof and Sherman, 2013; Prasad et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Analysis of synaptic terminal size confirmed sparser Cb innervation of the GPi overlap zone.
source: Furthermore, while our analysis of synaptic terminal size confirmed sparser Cb innervation of the GPi overlap zone (Deniau et al., 1992), we were unable to detect a difference in bouton size between the GPi overlap and non-overlap zones.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: The study was unable to detect a difference in bouton size between the GPi overlap and non-overlap zones.

claim: All data are consistent with Cb inputs being homogeneously drivers.
source: Collectively, all our data are consistent with Cb inputs being homogeneously drivers.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the anatomical and functional data.

claim: M1L5 and Cb inputs to motor thalamus transmit relevant information to be relayed to cortex.
source: We thus suggest that M1L5 and Cb inputs to motor thalamus transmit relevant information to be relayed to cortex; though, we also recognize that the GABAergic inputs from GPi and/or SNr are capable of blocking these strong excitatory drives, making future functional studies critical.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the driver properties of these inputs.

claim: The GABAergic inputs from GPi and/or SNr are capable of blocking the strong excitatory drives from M1L5 and Cb.
source: We thus suggest that M1L5 and Cb inputs to motor thalamus transmit relevant information to be relayed to cortex; though, we also recognize that the GABAergic inputs from GPi and/or SNr are capable of blocking these strong excitatory drives, making future functional studies critical.
evidence: This is an inference based on the convergence of inhibitory and excitatory inputs.

claim: The textbook view of the basal ganglia situates it within an information loop from cortex to basal ganglia to thalamus and back to cortex.
source: First, the textbook view of the basal ganglia situates it within an information loop from cortex to basal ganglia to thalamus and back to cortex (Kandel et al., 2020), though updates have been made (Haber and Mcfarland, 2001; Lanciego et al., 2012; Goldberg et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim describes the traditional view supported by a citation.

claim: The finding that basal ganglia inputs to motor thalamus impinge on relays receiving excitatory, driving input from either M1L5 or Cb pathways suggests a previously untested function of the basal ganglia—to gate information flow through motor thalamus.
source: However, our finding that basal ganglia inputs to motor thalamus impinge on relays receiving excitatory, driving input from either M1L5 or Cb pathways suggests a previously untested function of the basal ganglia—to gate information flow through motor thalamus.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Motor and frontal cortices are a major source of inputs to, as well as primary targets of, motor thalamic relays.
source: Motor and frontal cortices are a major source of inputs to, as well as primary targets of, motor thalamic relays (Bosch-Bouju et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bosch-Bouju et al., 2013.

claim: Thalamocortical connections can be reciprocal or non-reciprocal.
source: These thalamocortical connections can be reciprocal (Bosch-Bouju et al., 2013; Collins et al., 2018; Guo et al., 2018) or non-reciprocal (Rouiller et al., 1998; McFarland and Haber, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The study directly demonstrates the presence of a feedforward transthalamic pathway from M1, through VA/VL, to M2.
source: Indeed, here we directly demonstrate the presence of a feedforward transthalamic pathway from M1, through VA/VL, to M2 (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: In areas of the motor thalamus receiving convergent input from cortical L5 and basal ganglia, some fraction of which participates in transthalamic pathways, it is plausible that the basal ganglia can gate excitatory information between cortical regions.
source: Therefore, in areas of the motor thalamus receiving convergent input from cortical L5 and basal ganglia, some fraction of which participates in transthalamic pathways, it is plausible that the basal ganglia can gate excitatory information between cortical regions (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the study's findings.

source: When basal ganglia outputs are active, specific thalamic relays involved in transthalamic information transfer are inhibited.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the study's findings.

claim: Cortical areas have both direct and transthalamic connections organized in parallel.
source: Since cortical areas have both direct and transthalamic connections organized in parallel (Sherman and Guillery, 2013; Sherman, 2022), disconnecting the transthalamic excitatory stream allows only the direct, corticocortical pathway to persist.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: When thalamic relays are disinhibited due to upstream inhibition of the GPi or SNr, transthalamic transmission flows.
source: In contrast, when thalamic relays are disinhibited due to upstream inhibition of the GPi or SNr, transthalamic transmission flows (Figure 8A).

source: Thus, we reason that a potential function of basal ganglia inputs to some fraction of motor thalamic relays is to gate L5 signals, and thereby affect communication between cortical areas (Figure 8A).

source: Note that this offers a plausible and more detailed neuronal substrate for various ideas that the basal ganglia are involved in action selection (Redgrave et al., 1999; Redgrave et al., 2011; Gaidica et al., 2018; Park et al., 2020; Fiore et al., 2021).

claim: The data demonstrate that L5 of primary motor cortex (M1L5) drivers innervate cells receiving internal segment of the globus pallidus (GPi) and substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr) inputs.
source: That is, our data demonstrate that L5 of primary motor cortex (M1L5) drivers innervate cells receiving internal segment of the globus pallidus (GPi) and substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr) inputs.
evidence: This claim summarizes a key finding of the study.

claim: Given the organization where M1L5 drivers innervate cells receiving GPi and SNr inputs, M1L5 neurons could simultaneously disinhibit (via the basal ganglia loop) and drive (via the direct corticothalamic projection) motor thalamic relays.
source: Given this organization, M1L5 neurons could simultaneously disinhibit (via the basal ganglia loop, black arrows) and drive (via the direct corticothalamic projection, blue arrow) motor thalamic relays.

claim: The data advance understanding of basal ganglia function by demonstrating a direct projection from L5 of cortex to motor thalamic relays.
source: Third, our data advance understanding of basal ganglia function by demonstrating a direct projection from L5 of cortex, the starting point of the classical basal ganglia loop (Figure 8B, left), to the endpoint of the loop—motor thalamic relays.
evidence: This claim summarizes a key finding of the study.

claim: Some M1L5 axonal branches bypass the basal ganglia entirely.
source: In other words, some M1L5 axonal branches bypass the basal ganglia entirely (Figure 8B, right), which extends previous neuroanatomical data across species (Mooney and Konishi, 1991; Farries et al., 2005; Kita and Kita, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by the study's data and citations to prior work.

claim: Most, if not all, thalamic-projecting M1L5 neurons branch to innervate the caudoputamen.
source: Together with the findings that most, if not all, thalamic-projecting M1L5 neurons branch to innervate the caudoputamen (Economo et al., 2018; Jiang et al., 2020), the intriguing, albeit untested, possibility arises that a single M1L5 corticofugal neuron can affect motor thalamic activity indirectly through the classical basal ganglia loop (which is disinhibitory) as well as through the direct projection (excitatory).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.
